overview.text: Yellowstone National Park lies mainly in Wyoming, with portions in Montana and Idaho; established on March 1, 1872, it is recognized by the National Park Service as the world’s first national park. Its defining feature is an immense hydrothermal system: rain and snow seep underground, warm as groundwater circulates above a deep magma-storage region, and feed geysers, hot springs, mudpots, and steam vents. Old Faithful, in Upper Geyser Basin, erupts with unusual regularity, while Grand Prismatic Spring in Midway Geyser Basin is the park’s largest hot spring. Its vivid bands reflect heat-loving microorganisms living at different temperatures.

key_facts.text: Yellowstone was established on March 1, 1872; the National Park Service identifies it as the world’s first national park.
The park is 96% in Wyoming, 3% in Montana, and 1% in Idaho, according to National Park Service figures.
Yellowstone has more than 10,000 thermal features, including geysers, hot springs, mudpots, and steam vents.
A geyser erupts when heated water and steam build pressure in an underground reservoir and escape through a constricted passage; eruption intervals can vary.
Grand Prismatic Spring is Yellowstone’s largest hot spring; its colors come from heat-loving organisms adapted to different temperatures.
